To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

increasing adiposity, particularly fat cell size, results in impaired fat oxidation, ectopic storage of fat into liver, skeletal, and pancreatic tissue, and increased secretion of pro‐inflammatory cytokines and adipocytokines that result in insulin resistance and diabetes.
increased adipose tissue mass, increased fat cell volume, and failure to expand fat cell mass result in ectopic fat storage, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
increased fat intake, impaired fat oxidation, and the failure of fat cells to proliferate result in ectopic fat storage, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pathophysiological consequences of increased energy intake.
understanding the mechanisms by which increased adiposity leads to the development of insulin resistance, diabetes, and the associated complications.
the mechanisms that regulate the size of adipose tissue, with a particular emphasis on the mechanisms that regulate fat cell size and proliferation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the increased fat intake, impaired fat oxidation, and failure of fat cell proliferation result in ectopic fat storage, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes.

the development of ectopic fat storage in insulin‐sensitivetissues, such as skeletal muscle and liver, and/or in the beta cell, leads to insulin resistance and the pathophysiology underlying type 2 diabetes.
increased fat intake and decreased fat oxidation lead to failure to store fat in adipocytes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
increased fat intake, impaired fat oxidation, and failure of fat cell proliferation results in ectopic fat storage, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
increased fat intake leads to impaired fat oxidation and failure of adipose tissue to expand.

increasing adiposity, particularly with a high‐fat diet and impaired fat oxidation, leads to increased fat cell size and impaired fat cell proliferation and thus ectopic fat storage, which leads to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ectopic fat hypothesis and the adipose tissue endocrine function hypothesis are not mutually exclusive and may in fact work synergistically to produce the metabolic syndrome.
the development of ectopic fat storage, whether it is acquired or genetic, is a key step in the pathogenesis of the insulin resistance syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
increased energy intake and/or decreased energy expenditure leads to increased adiposity, which in turn leads to ectopic fat storage and increased secretion of adipokines.
